Headlines say the stock is down about 31% this year, and some ask why it fell on a Wednesday.
Several stories say investor Michael Burry added to his Adobe stake. That is one investor's choice, not a sign of what comes next.
Adobe launched new Firefly and Premiere mobile video tools, and won a patent case with OpenAI over content-labeling tech.

takeaways: Adobe is still growing. It had record sales and a raised forecast for the year.
Profit and cash did not keep pace with sales this quarter. Leadership is changing: the finance chief is interim and a new CEO is coming.
The big open question is AI. Adobe calls it a growth engine, but also names AI rivals as a top risk.

earnings.headline: Analog Devices had a record quarter: sales and profit both grew a lot compared with a year ago.
points: Revenue (sales) was $4.02 billion, up 40% from the same quarter last year. Data center and factory chips led the growth.
Profit per share was $2.74, up from $1.04 a year ago. They kept more of each sales dollar too: 67.3% vs 62.1%.
Guidance (their own forecast) for next quarter is sales of $4.3 billion, give or take $100 million. They warn results may differ.
They paid $1.7 billion back to shareholders this quarter through dividends (cash payouts) and buying back their own stock.
They design and make chips that sense, measure, connect and power things, used in factories, cars, phones and data centers.
In fiscal 2025, sales passed $11 billion, up 17%. Growth was broad, but sales in Japan fell 9%.
Factory-related chips are the biggest piece at 45% of sales. Cars are next at 30%.
Biggest named risks: US-China tension, export limits on sales to some Chinese companies, tariffs, and plants based abroad.
Some headlines say the stock fell along with other chip stocks, and one writer calls it too expensive if AI spending slows.
Others point to strong growth. Analysts publish price targets, which are opinions, not facts from the company.
Some 'ADI' headlines about a net loss or a plunge seem to be about ADI Global Distribution, a different company.

takeaways: The business is growing fast right now: more sales, more profit, and a higher forecast for next quarter.
A lot depends on demand for data centers and AI. If that spending slows, results could slow too.
China rules, tariffs and trade fights are real risks the company itself names. Read headlines carefully: not every 'ADI' is this company.

earnings.headline: ADP's sales and profit grew last quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Revenue (sales) rose 6% from a year ago to $5.5 billion.
Net earnings (profit) rose 11% to $1.1 billion; earnings per share rose 14% to $2.83.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up: sales growth of about 6% and adjusted EPS growth of 10% to 12% this year.
Weaker spots: PEO segment margin was flat, and they expect client revenue retention to slip by 10 to 30 basis points.
ADP sells payroll and HR software and services to more than 1.1 million clients, and earns interest on client money it holds.
Fiscal 2026 sales grew 7% to $21,947.4 million; interest on client funds rose to $1,354.8 million from $1,189.1 million.
They returned $4.7B to shareholders, including $2.6B of dividends and $2.1B of share buybacks.
Named risks: changes in laws and taxes, lower interest income on client funds, cyber breaches, and clients failing to pay PEO costs.
Several headlines compare ADP with its rival Paychex, including on dividends.
Some headlines note the stock rose 29% in a year. Past price moves do not predict future ones.
One headline links possible Social Security reform to renewed interest in ADP.

takeaways: The business grew steadily last quarter, and the company now expects a slightly better year than it did before.
Part of ADP's income comes from interest on client money it holds, so changes in interest rates can push results up or down.
Not everything improved: one division's margin was flat, and ADP expects to keep a bit less of its clients' business this year.

earnings.headline: Ameren earned more this quarter than a year ago and raised its own profit forecast for 2026.
points: Profit per share was $2.42, up from $2.17 a year ago once a one-time 2025 tax break is removed. Total sales were not in this release.
Profit was $676 million vs. $592 million adjusted a year earlier, helped by grid upgrades and a hot summer that raised power use.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 rose to $5.35 to $5.55 per share. For 2027 they expect $5.70 to $5.90.
Costs rose too: more tree trimming, plant upkeep and interest on debt. More shares also spread the profit thinner.
Ameren is a utility. It sells power to 2.5 million customers and gas to more than 900,000 in Missouri and Illinois.
Government boards set the prices it can charge. Profit depends on regulators letting it earn a return on what it builds.
New this year: Missouri gas rates filed after June 2026 may be based on expected future costs, not just past costs.
Biggest risk they name: delays. Rate cases can take up to 11 months, so prices can lag behind rising costs like inflation.
Ameren executive Theresa Shaw sold $57,725 of company stock. Another officer gave away 445 shares and still holds 19,875.
Ameren presented its plans at the EEI Financial Conference, an industry meeting for utility investors.

takeaways: Profit grew this quarter, mostly from building and upgrading the power grid, plus warm weather that raised electricity use.
Ameren plans $38.1 billion of grid spending and forecasts 8% to 10% yearly profit-per-share growth, 2027 through 2031. It's a forecast, not a promise.
Costs and interest on debt are rising, and regulators control its prices, so results depend heavily on government rate decisions.

points: A report says AP Aguila holds a stake in Grupo Aeromexico, but limits apply to how many votes that stake can cast.
A headline says Wall Street analysts gave Aeromexico an average rating; that is opinion, not company news.
Most other AERO headlines are about different companies with a similar name, not this airline.

takeaways: No new official earnings report or annual report text was provided here, so there are no sales or profit numbers to explain.
The main real news is about who owns part of the company and the voting limits on that stake.
Many AERO headlines are about other companies, so check that news is about the airline before reading into it.

earnings.headline: AES earned more in Q3 2025 than a year earlier and kept its own forecast for the year unchanged.
points: Profit (net income) was $517 million, up from $215 million in Q3 2024, helped a lot by selling tax credits.
Adjusted EPS (the company's own cleaned-up profit per share) was $0.75, up from $0.71 a year earlier.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2025 adjusted EPS stays at $2.10 to $2.26.
Weaker side: lower power output in its Energy Infrastructure unit and the sale of AES Brasil held results back.
AES makes money making and delivering electricity: solar, wind, batteries, older fuel plants, and utilities in Indiana and Ohio.
2025 profit (net income) fell to $162 million from $802 million, partly because 2024 had a one-time gain from selling AES Brasil.
Sales (revenue) slipped $45 million to 12,233 million dollars; adjusted EBITDA (core operating earnings) rose to $2,871 million.
Risks they name: plant outages, equipment failure, storms, cyber-attacks, and lithium-ion battery fires that could bring lawsuits.

takeaways: The latest quarter looked better than a year earlier, and the company kept its yearly forecast.
For full-year 2025, reported profit dropped sharply, even though core operating earnings grew.
Much of the growth comes from new solar, wind and battery projects, including power deals with data centers.

earnings.headline: Aflac's profit fell sharply this quarter, mostly from losses on investments it sold, while its U.S. insurance business earned more.
points: Total revenues (sales) were $3.3 billion, down from $4.7 billion a year ago.
Net earnings (profit) were $303 million vs $1.6 billion a year ago, mainly from losses when selling investments.
Adjusted earnings (profit without one-off items) fell 8.5% to $1.2 billion. The release gives no forecast for next quarter.
Japan pretax profit fell 21.0% to $961 million, while U.S. pretax profit rose 31.5% to $493 million.
Aflac sells health and cancer insurance in Japan and the U.S., and also earns money investing the premiums (payments) customers make.
In 2025, Aflac Japan's pretax profit slipped 1.5% to $3,440 million as its premiums fell 2.7%.
Biggest named risk: the yen vs the dollar. A weaker yen means fewer dollars get reported from the Japan business.
A sharp jump in the yen could strain the parent company's cash because of its currency hedges (protection contracts).
Japan Post Holdings, a 10% owner of Aflac, sold some of its Aflac shares, per Investing.com.
Other headlines compare Aflac's dividend with MetLife's and point out its lower quarterly earnings.

takeaways: The big profit drop came mostly from selling investments at a loss, not from the day-to-day insurance business.
Japan, its biggest market, is shrinking in sales and profit, while the U.S. business is growing.
The dividend (cash paid to owners) is $0.61 per share, and Aflac has raised it 44 years in a row.

earnings.headline: Affirm's sales and profit grew strongly this quarter, though its own borrowing costs ticked up from last quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) grew 35% to $1,262 million. Total spending through Affirm (GMV) grew 34% to $14.4 billion.
Profit from operations was $187M, up 194%. It was the 8th straight quarter of profit under standard accounting rules.
Weak spots: fees from stores grew only 23%, slower than spending, and their own borrowing costs rose from last quarter.
Card spending grew 117% to $3.3 billion. They expect the first Affirm Edge tests to start in the first half of 2027.
They make money from fees stores pay, interest on some loans, and selling loans to investors. They charge $0 in late fees.
They had about 571 thousand active stores as of June 30, 2026, and made $9.5 billion of loans directly that year.
Risk: they rely on two banks, Celtic Bank and Lead Bank, to make almost all loans. Losing them would hurt.
Other named risks: higher interest rates, a weaker economy, loans not being paid back, and relying on a few big partners.
Several headlines say the stock has been falling, with one tying the drop to an insider (company leader) selling shares.
One headline says the stock looks near fair value after a 168% run.
An investment manager reported owning an 18 million-share stake in the company.

takeaways: The business is growing fast and making a profit, with sales up 35% from a year ago.
Its card is the big growth engine, but higher interest rates raise what Affirm pays to borrow.
Affirm depends on a few banks and partners, and on people paying loans back; trouble there would hurt.

earnings.headline: C3 AI's sales were lower than a year ago, but losses shrank, cash flow turned positive, and new deals rose 73% from last quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) were $52.4 million, lower than the same quarter last year.
Still losing money: adjusted operating loss was $36.2 million, 33% better than last quarter. Adjusted means some costs are left out.
More cash came in than went out: free cash flow was $2.1 million. Cash and investments on hand: $651.1 million.
Their own forecast (guidance): next quarter sales of $51.0 to $55.0 million, full year $210.0 to $240.0 million.
They sell business AI software, mostly by subscription, which made up 91% of sales last fiscal year.
Last fiscal year sales were $250.3 million, a 35.7% drop. They blame a sales shake-up, the CEO's health and weak execution.
They have lost money every year since 2009. Last year's net loss was about $470.4 million.
Big risk: a few large customers bring in much of the money, and those customers don't have to renew.
Most headlines are about the wider AI stock market swinging lower, not about C3 AI itself.
Much of the news covers Anthropic's IPO (its first sale of shares to the public).

takeaways: Sales are smaller than a year ago, but the company is spending less, so its losses are getting smaller.
It still loses money, and its full-year forecast is below last year's sales.
It has a large pile of cash and investments, and new signed deals picked up from last quarter.

earnings.headline: AIG sold more insurance and reported higher profit, but its core insurance profit fell as storm claims rose.
points: Premiums (money customers pay for insurance) were $6.7 billion, up 7% from a year ago, led by business and personal insurance.
Net income (profit) rose to $844 million from $519 million, mostly because the value of its investments changed.
Adjusted profit, which leaves out those investment swings, fell to $1.1 billion from $1.2 billion. That is worse.
Storm claims hit $283 million vs $100 million a year ago. Profit from selling insurance (underwriting income) was $564 million.
AIG makes money by charging premiums for insurance and investing that money until it has to pay claims.
Its biggest named risk: claims coming in higher than expected, so its reserves (money set aside for claims) fall short.
It also names big disasters and terrorism as risks. Its largest terrorism exposure is in New York City.
It purchases reinsurance (insurance for insurance companies) to limit losses from big events.
Several articles look back at how AIG stock did over the last 5 years and ask whether it is fairly valued.
One piece says insurers like AIG may see more demand for D&O cover (insurance that protects company leaders from lawsuits).
Insurance broker Aon closed a $17.0 billion deal for USI, a sign that companies in the insurance industry keep merging.

takeaways: AIG is growing. It sold more insurance this quarter in every main part of its business.
Profit from its core insurance work dropped, mainly because storms cost more than they did last year.
It paid $787 million back to owners through dividends and share repurchases, and declared a $0.50 dividend per share.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 6% to $1.122 billion, but profit fell as Akamai spent heavily to build out its cloud business.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.122 billion, up 6%. Security sales rose 9% and cloud infrastructure sales jumped 34%.
Profit fell. Net income per share was $0.77, down 21%. Their adjusted figure was $1.77, down 5%.
The older delivery business shrank to $391 million, down 3%. Profit kept from each sale (operating margin) fell 6 percentage points.
Guidance (their own forecast) is sales growth of 17% to 22% in 2027 and over $7.0 billion in sales in 2028.
They sell three things: security against cyberattacks, cloud computing, and delivery (moving web content fast).
Security brings in the most money. They run more than 4,300 network sites in over 130 countries.
A risk they name: delivery sales keep falling because of price cuts and customers doing the work themselves.
Other risks: tough rivals, rising data-center costs driven by giant cloud firms, tariffs and world events.
Akamai planned a $2.2B convertible debt offering (borrowing that can turn into shares) to fund cloud growth.
Evercore downgraded the stock over worries about that borrowing. Other headlines mentioned cloud delays.
The stock also rose 9% one day on management's upbeat AI outlook.

takeaways: Akamai is growing, led by cloud and security, but its profit is shrinking for now as it spends heavily to build.
Management points to $14 billion in multi-year cloud deals signed this year and forecasts faster growth for 2027.
The company is borrowing a lot to pay for this growth, so the plan has to work out for the debt to make sense.

points: Alcon's Q3 profit beat expectations, but sales (revenue) came in below what experts expected. The stock fell.
Alcon narrowed its '26 outlook (its own forecast), and a tighter eye-care market raised worries about slower growth.
Sales of implantable lenses were weak and it lost US premium lens share. It is betting on Vivity Pro to grow again.

takeaways: Profit looked fine, but sales missed. That gap is why the stock fell about 5% after the report.
The weak spot is lenses put in during eye surgery. Premium lenses did better, but Alcon lost some US share.
Seven years after splitting from Novartis, its record is called mixed. Some analysts cut targets, others stayed positive.

earnings.headline: Sales grew a little from a year ago and profit rose, but scanner sales fell and sales dipped from last quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.015 billion, up 1.9% from a year ago but down 3.9% from last quarter.
Clear aligner sales rose 4.2% to $839.3 million. Scanner and software sales fell 7.6% to $175.5 million.
Profit per share was $1.90, up from $0.78 a year ago. Fuel costs for shipping and lower aligner prices hurt margins a bit.
Their own forecast (guidance) for Q4 is $1,000M to $1,020M in sales. They expect weak spending on dental care to continue.
They make Invisalign clear aligners (about 80% of sales) plus iTero mouth scanners and exocad dental software (the other 20%).
Over 22 million people have been treated with Invisalign. Teens and kids make up about 70% of orthodontic case starts.
In 2025 they added new iTero Lumina scanners and kept investing in AI tools to make treatment faster and more accurate.
Biggest named risks: a weak economy makes people skip teeth straightening; currency swings, tariffs and shipping costs also hurt.
The company announced a $270 Million deal to buy back its own shares.
The CEO and CFO are set to speak at an event in London on Nov. 17.
Some headlines note the stock lagged its competitors on one recent trading day.

takeaways: More people are getting Invisalign, but each case brings in a bit less money and scanner sales are shrinking.
Profit improved a lot from a year ago, and the company says tight cost control helped.
The company is spending heavily to buy back its own shares while saying dental spending is still soft.

earnings.headline: Allegion grew sales and profit in Q3, led by its Americas business, and raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1,172.6 million, up 9.6%. Leaving out deals and currency swings, sales rose 7.2%.
Profit per share (EPS) was $2.59, up 18.8%. Adjusted EPS (one-offs removed) was $2.60, up 13.0%.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): 2026 adjusted EPS of $9.05 to $9.10, and sales growth of 9.5% to 10.5%.
Weak spot: International sales fell 0.2% before deals, and its margin (profit per $ of sales) slipped 40 basis points to 13.9%.
Allegion makes locks, door closers, exit devices, steel doors and access-control systems, with brands like Schlage and Von Duprin.
2025 sales were $4,067.3 million, up 7.8%, helped by higher prices and companies they bought.
They bought ELATEC, a German access-tech maker, on July 1, 2025. Deals done in 2025 cost about $631.6 million.
Risks they name: US tariffs (about 20-25% of product costs come from Mexico), tax disputes in many countries, environmental costs.
Several headlines are opinion pieces arguing for the stock. These are outside views, not facts from the company.
Filings show large investors hold stakes, such as a passive investor reporting 3.24 million shares.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew this quarter, mostly from the Americas, and the company raised its own 2026 forecast.
Part of reported profit came from one-time tariff refunds ($19.9 million). The adjusted numbers leave that out.
Not everything improved: the International business shrank slightly and its margin fell. Total debt was $2,032.0 million.

earnings.headline: Ally earned more than a year ago, but it set aside much more money for car loans that may go bad.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.3 billion. Profit for common shareholders was $401 million, up from $371 million a year ago.
Profit per share (EPS) was $1.30, up 10% year over year.
Money set aside for bad loans rose $114 million to $529 million. The car loan unit's pre-tax profit fell $84 million.
Record 4.8 million car loan applications, up 20%. But loans 30+ days late rose to 4.96%.
Ally is an online-only bank plus a large car loan and car insurance business. It also lends to mid-sized companies.
It had $196.0 billion in assets (what it owns) at the end of 2025.
It sold its credit card business and stopped making new home loans in 2025, so that loan pile will shrink.
Risks they name: unpaid car loans, low used car prices, interest rate changes, and leaning heavily on GM and Stellantis dealers.
Analyst articles note the stock has risen 51% and debate whether it is fairly valued.
Ally is scheduled to present at the J.P. Morgan Financials Conference.

takeaways: Ally made more money than a year ago, mostly by lending more.
It is putting aside more money for loans that may not be paid back, and late payments ticked up.
Its results depend on car sales and on everyday borrowers paying their bills.

earnings.headline: Medicine sales grew fast, but rising costs meant profit from running the business went down.
points: Medicine sales (revenue) hit $1,292 million, up 52% from a year ago, led by its heart-and-nerve drug AMVUTTRA.
Operating income (profit from running the business) fell 6%. Cost of goods rose to 28.0% of sales from 23.2%.
Partner income fell 80%. Last year included a one-time $300.0 million payment from Roche that did not repeat.
They say they're on track for their 2026 forecast (guidance). New drug nucresiran could launch by 2030 if approved.
They make money selling six approved RNAi medicines (drugs that switch off disease-causing genes), plus partner deals and royalties.
2025 was their first profitable year, with about $3.0 billion in medicine sales, but past losses add up to $6.70 billion.
They pay Sanofi a royalty (a cut of sales) on AMVUTTRA that rises to 30% of sales above $1.50 billion, which squeezes margins.
Biggest risks they name: relying on AMVUTTRA, trials that may fail, drug pricing rules, and patent fights.
The stock hit a 52-week low of 149.17 USD, and one headline describes a 64% drop.
One report says shares rose around 5.5% after the quarter. Analysts cut their price targets to $279 and $283.79.
An investment manager reported owning over 10% of the company.

takeaways: The main heart drug, AMVUTTRA, is selling much faster than last year and drives most of the growth.
Costs rose and the company leans heavily on one drug, a risk it names itself.
Reported net income jumped over 500%, but this excerpt doesn't explain why, so don't read it as normal profit.

earnings.headline: Applied Materials had record sales of $10.41 billion this quarter, up 53 percent from a year ago.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $10.41 billion, up 53 percent from the same quarter last year.
Profit per share (EPS) was $3.40 on the official GAAP basis and $4.16 on their adjusted basis, up 43 percent and 92 percent.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: about $11,100 million in sales, give or take $500 million.
Not all good: a small 'Other' group still lost money, $21 million this quarter and $229 million for the full year.
They make the machines chip factories use to build semiconductors (computer chips) found in phones, PCs, cars and AI servers.
Most sales come from chipmaking machines; a second group (AGS) sells repairs, spare parts and factory software.
In fiscal 2025, about 89% of their sales went to customers outside the United States.
Biggest risks they name: chip demand swings up and down, AI spending is hard to predict, and U.S. export limits on China.
Headlines say results beat Wall Street targets, yet some report the stock fell over 5% after the release.
Some writers say the stock looks pricey after a 127% run; one trimmed its fair-value estimate over profit-margin worries.
Several stories credit strong demand for AI chips as the main reason sales are growing.

takeaways: Business is strong right now: record sales and profit for the year, driven mostly by demand for AI chips.
The company expects next quarter to be bigger still, but that is their own forecast, not a promise.
Risks are real: the chip business runs in cycles, AI spending can change fast, and China export rules limit some sales.

earnings.headline: AMD had a record quarter, led by its AI data center chips, but gaming chip sales fell sharply.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year ago.
Profit (net income) was $2.4 billion. Data Center sales nearly doubled, up 97% to $8.5 billion.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: about $17 billion in sales, plus or minus 3%.
Bad news: gaming sales fell 40% to $773 million, pulling the Client and Gaming group down 8%.
AMD makes computer chips for data centers, PCs, game consoles, and things like cars and factory machines.
In 2025 it pushed hard into AI data center chips and signed a deal to supply OpenAI with 6 gigawatts of GPUs.
Risks they name: tough rivals, boom-and-bust chip cycles, export rules, and relying on outside factories to make chips.
A small number of big customers bring in much of the money. Losing one could hurt the business badly.
Headlines are split: some writers expect the stock to bounce back, others ask how far it could fall.
Many stories are about why the share price jumped or dropped on a given day, not about the business itself.

takeaways: AI chips for data centers are now AMD's main growth engine, and they grew fast this quarter.
Not everything is up: gaming chip sales dropped hard, and the company says so in its own report.
AMD expects more growth next quarter, but forecasts can miss, and the company lists many risks that could change things.

earnings.headline: AMETEK had record sales of $2.22 billion, up 17%, and raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (money from customers) hit a record $2.22 billion, up 17% from the same quarter a year ago.
Profit per share was $1.85 by standard rules, or $2.21 on the company's adjusted view, which leaves out deal costs.
They raised their guidance (own forecast): adjusted profit per share of $8.53 to $8.57 for 2026, up from $8.20 to $8.30.
Worse: interest paid on borrowing rose to $39,822 thousand from $22,514 thousand, as debt grew to pay for a big purchase.
They make precise instruments and machine parts for factories, power, planes, defense and hospitals, in two groups.
2025 sales were a record $7,401.1 million, up 6.6%; 4% came from buying companies, only 2% from core sales.
They bought two companies in 2025, Kern and FARO, spending $933.2 million.
Risks they name: tariffs, swings in interest rates and foreign money values, and fitting in companies they buy.
Most headlines are stock-price pages and analyst price targets, not news about the business itself.
One analyst piece says growth is strong, but more debt and a high stock price could hold it back.

takeaways: The business is growing fast: record sales and profit, and they raised their own forecast for the year.
A big part of the growth comes from buying other companies, paid for with much more borrowed money.
Long-term debt jumped from 1,074,334 to 6,029,565 (thousands of dollars) since December 2025, so interest costs are rising.

earnings.headline: Ameriprise grew sales and profit this quarter, but clients pulled money from its fund business and one insurance unit earned less.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 10 percent to $5.1 billion, mostly because clients had more money with the company.
Profit per share was $12.32 under standard accounting rules, up from $9.33 a year ago.
Bad news: clients took a net $9.3 billion out of its fund business, mostly big institutions moving money elsewhere.
It expects about $32 billion of Huntington Bank client money to move onto its platform through mid-2027.
It makes money mainly from fees on clients' money, through a network of more than 10,000 financial advisors.
Its main customers are households with $500,000 to $5,000,000 to invest.
It looked after $1.7 trillion at the end of 2025. That grew to $1.8 trillion by this latest quarter.
Biggest risk it names: when markets fall, client balances shrink and so do its fees. Many fund clients can leave on short notice.
Several headlines say the stock rose 86% and debate whether it is still cheap. Those are opinions, not facts from the company.
Oklahoma's largest credit union moved its financial advice program to Ameriprise.
It was named a Military Friendly employer for the thirteenth year in a row.

takeaways: The core advice business is growing: more client money, more sales and higher profit.
The fund arm is shrinking in new money, as investors keep leaving active fund managers.
It is buying back a lot of its own shares, so profit per share can rise faster than total profit.

earnings.headline: Alpha lost less money than last quarter and sold more coal, but costs kept rising and core earnings were lower than a year ago.
points: Sales from the main coal business were $560.6 million, up from $491.5 million last quarter. They sold 3.9 million tons vs 3.5.
They still lost money: a net loss (profit after all costs) of $9.3 million, smaller than the $12.3 million loss last quarter.
Cost to produce rose to $106.93 per ton from $103.07. Core earnings (Adjusted EBITDA) were $29.4 million vs $41.7 million a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2027: ship 14.3 million to 15.7 million tons. A June storm damaged key equipment at a port they use.
Alpha mines metallurgical coal (coal used to make steel) in Virginia and West Virginia and sells it to steelmakers around the world.
Coal reserves (coal it plans to mine) slipped to 294,486 thousand tons in 2025 from 298,639 thousand.
Risk they name: fuel costs. They expected to buy about 22.0 million gallons of diesel in 2026, and higher prices could hurt results.
Risk they name: a strong U.S. dollar can let foreign coal rivals offer lower prices to overseas customers.
Headlines say the stock hit a 52-week low (lowest price in a year) at 132.44 USD.
Some analysts are cautious: one group's average rating is "Reduce," and one article argues the stock looks 24% overvalued.
A filing shows a passive investor now owns more than 5% of the company.

takeaways: The company is still losing money each quarter, though the loss shrank from $12.3 million to $9.3 million.
Rising costs per ton are the main problem the CEO points to; storm damage at a port adds uncertainty for 2027.
Its money cushion looks solid: $334.1 million in cash and only $10.6 million in long-term debt (money owed).

earnings.headline: Sales grew a little and they raised their full-year forecast, but profit fell.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 2.5% to $2,785 million. Cash sales from data centers jumped 16.3%.
Profit (net income) fell 14.4% to $781 million, partly because of losses on investments they hold.
They raised their own sales forecast (guidance) by $55 million, but cut their profit forecast by $30 million.
Rent growth from existing towers was just 1.1%. They bought back $315 million of stock and approved $2.0 billion more.
They rent space on 149,686 towers and sites to phone and TV companies, plus 30 data centers (computer buildings) in the US.
Leases usually last five to ten years, and US rent rises about 3% a year, so most sales repeat.
Risk: AT&T Mexico (about $300 million of 2025 rent) is fighting its lease. Part of that rent sits in a locked escrow account.
Risk: DISH stopped paying on its tower deal and was in default as of January 2026. American Tower took it to court.
Reports say bankrupt DISH Wireless reached a $525M settlement with American Tower over the tower deal.
The company sold new bonds (borrowed money). One report says that brings in $1.47 billion after costs.
Analysts are writing about the stock, and Deutsche Bank started covering it.

takeaways: Sales grew a little, but reported profit fell. The company says investment losses were a main reason.
Data centers are the fastest-growing part. Rent from existing towers barely grew.
Debt is large (4.9x yearly cash earnings), and fights with big customers like AT&T Mexico and DISH are a real risk.

earnings.headline: Sales and business profit grew strongly, but bottom-line profit dipped and heavy AI spending turned cash flow negative.
points: Sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion vs $180.2 billion a year earlier. AWS, the cloud arm (renting computers online), grew 39%.
Operating income (profit from running the business) jumped to $28.1 billion from $17.4 billion, a 13.9% margin, their highest ever.
Net income (bottom-line profit) slipped to $20.7 billion from $21.2 billion, as last year had a $9.5 billion Anthropic investment gain.
Free cash flow (cash left after spending) became an outflow of $42.4 billion, mostly from AI spending. CEO projects AWS growth over 40%.
Amazon makes money selling products, taking a cut from outside sellers, and from cloud computing, ads and subscriptions.
They expect tech and infrastructure spending to keep rising, including for AI, which can hurt short-term cash flow.
Shares plus stock awards rose to 11.0 billion at end of 2025 from 10.9 billion a year before, so each share is slightly diluted.
Biggest risks named: tough competition, new bets like AI and satellites not paying off, and international, tariff and trade troubles.
Recent stories say the stock fell after Q3 results and has since won back those losses.
UBS, a big bank, lowered its rating on the stock, even as the shares bounced back.
Headlines also focus on how much Amazon's stake in Anthropic, an AI company, could be worth.

takeaways: The main businesses are growing and earning more, with the cloud arm AWS leading the way.
Amazon is spending huge sums on AI, so right now more cash is going out than coming in.
The strong cloud forecast is the company's own view; the AI spending still has to pay off, and they call results unpredictable.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped 58.5% from a year ago to about $3.66 billion, beating the company's own forecast of $3.3 billion.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3.66 billion, up 58.5% from a year ago and up 20.5% from the quarter before.
Profit per share was $1.22, up from $0.67 a year ago. The CFO called it record net income.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $3.9 - $4.0 billion and profit per share of $1.26 - $1.30.
One thing slipped: they kept 63.6% of each sale after product costs (gross margin), down from 64.6% a year ago.
They sell network gear and software that link data centers, AI systems, offices and wide networks together.
Last year about 65% of sales came from AI, cloud and data center gear, 18% from campus and routing, 17% from software and services.
Big risk they name: a few buyers. One customer was 26% of sales and another was 16% last year.
Other risks: key parts come from few suppliers, one main chip vendor, tariffs, China export limits, and hard-to-forecast AI demand.
Most headlines are about the share price itself: a 5% drop on one day, a rally on another.
Some articles debate whether the stock is overvalued after the higher forecast. These are opinions, not company news.

takeaways: The business is growing fast and earning record profit, mostly from networks built for AI.
It leans on a handful of huge customers and a few key suppliers, so sales can swing if any of them pull back.
The company expects more growth next quarter, but it also warns sales are bumpy and AI demand's long-term path is unknown.

earnings.headline: Aon's sales grew 3% and adjusted profit rose, but reported operating profit slipped 1% this quarter.
points: Revenue (sales) rose 3% to $4.1 billion. Organic growth (from businesses they already had, not deals) was 6%.
Profit per share was $2.23, up from $2.11. Their adjusted measure (leaving out one-off items) was $3.36, up 10%.
Operating income (profit from the main business) fell 1% to $809 million, hurt by restructuring costs that rose 191%.
Human Capital sales fell 4%, mostly from selling a unit. Aon expects the USI purchase to close soon and will pay down debt first.
Aon earns fees for advising on risk, insurance, health benefits and retirement for clients in more than 120 countries.
In 2025, revenue rose 9% to $17.2 billion and diluted profit per share was $17.02, up from $12.49.
Part of 2025's profit jump came from a one-time $1.2 billion gain on selling the NFP Wealth business.
Risks they name: a weaker economy, tough competition, currency swings, their debt, disasters and cyberattacks.
Several headlines say Aon completed its $17 billion purchase of USI, growing its reach with mid-sized U.S. businesses.
Some analysts raised their price targets after the USI deal. These are opinions, not facts about the business.

takeaways: Sales and adjusted profit kept growing, though reported operating profit dipped slightly this quarter.
The big USI purchase adds reach but also adds debt; Aon says paying that debt down comes first.
Aon bought back none of its own shares this quarter while it focuses on the deal and its debt.

earnings.headline: Air Products sold more and grew its adjusted profit last quarter, beating its own forecast, but costs rose and one-time charges hit results.
points: Sales for the quarter were $3.6 billion, up 12 percent. Full-year sales were $13.0 billion, up eight percent.
Adjusted earnings per share (profit per share, minus one-off items) were $3.61, up six percent, above the middle of their forecast.
Bad news: costs rose, and charges for exiting projects, mainly two China coal plants, held official profit to $2.62 per share.
Their own forecast for fiscal 2027: adjusted EPS of $14.15 to $14.50, and $3.0 billion to $3.5 billion spent on plants and equipment.
They make and sell industrial gases like hydrogen. About half of sales come from long-term contracts to supply gas on-site.
Fiscal 2025 was a reset year: a new CEO cancelled or shrank several big clean-energy projects to focus on the core gas business.
That year sales of $12.0 billion fell 1%, and about $3.7 billion in charges led to a loss of $1.74 per share.
Risks they name: weaker economies, less demand for clean hydrogen, tariffs, and about 60% of sales coming from outside the US.
Reports say quarterly results beat Wall Street estimates, helped by higher volumes (more gas sold).
Air Products plans to nominate Carol Williams, who spent 34 years at Dow, to its board of directors.

takeaways: The core gas business is growing again: more sales and higher adjusted profit than a year ago.
Costs are rising, and leaving old projects still costs money, so official profit stays well below adjusted profit.
The company is spending less on new plants and gave its own forecast for next year, but forecasts can miss.

earnings.headline: Sales held about steady from a year ago, but profit fell as Tesla spent much more on AI, robots and new factories.
points: Sales (revenue) were 28,046 million dollars, about flat vs 28,095 a year ago. Energy storage sales fell to 2,881 from 3,415.
Profit fell: net income (what's left after all costs) was 787 million dollars, down from 1,373 a year earlier.
The business brought in $6.3B of cash, but heavy factory and AI spending left free cash flow at $1.5B, down from 3,990 million.
No number forecast (guidance) given. They aim to run factories at full use and expect AI, software and robotaxi profits to grow.
Tesla makes money selling and leasing electric cars, plus big batteries for homes and power grids, and software like FSD (Supervised).
In 2025 sales were $94.83 billion, down $2.86 billion. Net income was $3.79 billion, down $3.30 billion from the year before.
They delivered about 1.64 million cars in 2025 and ended the year with $44.06 billion in cash and investments.
Biggest risks they name: tariffs, part shortages, delays on new products like Cybercab and robots, and the end of EV tax credits.

takeaways: The car business is holding steady, but profits are thinner because Tesla is spending heavily on AI, robots and factories.
Tesla still has a large cash cushion and says the business generally pays for its own spending.
Big bets like robotaxis and the Optimus robot are just starting; Tesla itself warns they could face delays.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit grew, and the company nudged up its yearly profit forecast, but cash flow was weaker than last year.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $1.3 billion, up 7.6% from a year ago. The engineering unit grew 14.1%.
Profit was $110.4 million, or $2.97 per share, up 12.7% from a year ago.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) to $11.70 to $12.20 profit per share, mostly because buybacks left fewer shares.
Worse: free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) fell to $73.4 million, lower than last year.
They sell and repair industrial parts like bearings, hydraulics and factory automation from about 580 locations.
Two units: Service Center fixes urgent breakdowns; Engineered Solutions designs systems to make factories run better.
Biggest risk they name: if factories slow down, they buy fewer parts, and prices and profits get squeezed.
Other risks: supply chain breaks, customers not paying bills, big customers or suppliers merging, and tough competition.
Most headlines are stock-picking opinion pieces and option price charts, not news about the business itself.
One headline looks at the company through its cash flow; none report new events at the company.

takeaways: Sales and profit both grew this quarter, and the company says October sales were up about 10% so far.
Cash coming in was weaker than last year, and cash on hand dipped while debt rose a bit as they bought back shares.
Their forecast is not a promise: they warn inflation, trade policy and world events could hurt results.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit rose a lot this quarter, mostly because of companies they bought, and this release gives no new forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3,930 million vs $3,325 million. Only 5% growth came from the old business. The rest came from buying firms.
Profit (net earnings) was $406 million vs $273 million. Profit per share rose to $1.55 from $1.04.
This release gives no forecast (guidance). The CEO said it was their 26th straight quarter of double-digit adjusted profit growth.
Watch-out: last year's quarter had about $76 million of extra interest income. Some bonus fees (contingent) did not grow at all.
They are an insurance middleman (broker). They help clients buy insurance and handle claims, but don't carry the insurance risk.
About 67% of sales come from the U.S. and 33% from abroad, mainly Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the U.K.
In 2025 they bought AssuredPartners for $13.8 billion. Reported profit per share fell 12% to $5.74 from $6.50.
Big risks they name: a weak economy, not being able to keep buying firms, AI, cyberattacks, and their debt.
Company insiders sold shares. CFO Douglas K. Howell sold 5,000 shares and still holds 87,961 directly.
Insider William Ziebell sold 23,510 shares. Insiders sell for many reasons; it is not a forecast.
A Seeking Alpha writer called the latest quarter strong.

takeaways: The company is growing fast, but mostly by buying other insurance brokers, not by its old business growing.
Profit is up this year, but full-year profit per share went down last year, partly because of deal costs.
Buying many firms brings risks: more debt, merging teams, and deals that may not work out. The company names these itself.

earnings.headline: APA pumped more oil than it planned, earned $698 million, and raised its 2026 cash forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2,769 million this quarter, up from $2,115 million in the same quarter a year earlier.
Profit was $698 million, or $2.00 per share. U.S. oil output beat their own forecast (guidance).
They now expect about $2.9 billion of free cash flow (cash left after spending) in 2026, up $600 million.
Downside: Egypt output came in slightly below forecast, and expected running costs rose $25 million to $1,525 million.
They make money by finding and pumping oil and natural gas, mainly in the U.S. and Egypt.
In 2025, cash from operations was $4.5 billion, up $925 million, mostly from collecting money owed and lower costs.
They ran 19 drilling rigs on average in 2025, down from 22, and sold $611 million of smaller assets.
Risks they name: swinging oil and gas prices, bigger rivals, and stricter rules on fracking and methane.
Headlines note the stock rose 102% and debate whether it is still cheap. Opinions differ.
Coverage highlights the raised $2.9B free cash flow forecast after the third-quarter results.
Some writers point to Suriname as a future cash source. One analyst lowered its rating.

takeaways: This quarter went well: more oil than planned, higher sales, and a bigger yearly cash forecast.
They are using cash to pay down debt and buy back shares, cutting yearly interest costs by more than $180 million.
Results depend on oil and gas prices, which swing. Egypt fell a bit short of plan and running costs rose.

earnings.headline: APi posted record sales and profit this quarter and raised its own forecast for the year, but it kept a smaller share of each sale.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.6 billion, up 22.5% from a year ago. Not counting companies it bought, growth was 15.7%.
Profit (net income) was $114 million, up 22.6%. A wider profit measure, adjusted EBITDA, was $350 million, up 24.6%.
Bad news: gross margin (share of sales left after direct costs) fell to 30.1% from 31.3%, hit by rising material and fuel costs.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 sales rose to $9,200 to $9,250 million, up from $8,875 to $9,025 million in July.
They inspect, service and install fire safety, security, elevator and escalator systems. The law requires much of this work.
Growth comes partly from buying companies: 14 deals in 2025 for $233 million, and 140 acquisitions since 2005.
Risks they name: tariffs raising material costs, higher labor costs, supply problems, and a costly new company-wide computer system.
Business is seasonal: sales are usually lower in the first half of the year because bad weather delays projects.
Most headlines are stock quote pages and opinion pieces about the stock, not new company news.
APi said it will speak at a UBS conference for industrial and transportation companies.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew fast, and the company raised its own forecast for the full year.
Material and fuel costs are rising, so the company keeps less of each sales dollar after direct costs.
Part of the growth comes from buying other companies, which adds risk if those deals don't work out.

earnings.headline: AppLovin had a record quarter: sales rose 55% to $2.18 billion and profit rose 72% to $1.44 billion.
points: Revenue (sales) was $2.18 billion this quarter, up 55% from a year ago.
Net income (profit after all costs) grew 72% to $1.44 billion. That is a 66% net income margin.
Guidance (their own forecast) for next quarter: sales of $2,365 to $2,395 million, in millions as reported.
Costs also went up, and research spending more than doubled. They repurchased 4.1 million shares for $1.4 billion.
They make money from ad tools: apps pay to find users, and AppLovin earns when ads hit the advertiser's return goals.
In 2025 they sold their own games (Apps) business for $400 million in cash plus about 20% of the buyer, Tripledot.
Named risks: results can swing a lot, reliance on other platforms, and new privacy, AI and advertising laws.
They also name their debt, relying on a few key people, and founders keeping voting control as risks.
Headlines say the stock jumped sharply after the results, then fell on some days, like a 3.23% drop at the open on Nov 10.
Reuters reports, citing sources, that AppLovin is among firms in talks to acquire Criteo, another ad tech company.
One analysis says upgrades to its Axon AI ad engine helped growth, but competition is still a risk.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew fast this quarter, and the company expects next quarter's sales to be higher still.
The business depends on ads inside apps, so other platforms, new laws or competition could hurt it.
The stock has swung hard both ways; the company itself warns its results can rise and fall from quarter to quarter.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit grew strongly this quarter, but the business used cash instead of bringing it in.
points: Total revenue (sales) was $234.6 million, up 25% from a year ago. Cloud subscriptions grew 20% to $136.4 million.
Profit rose: GAAP net income (official profit) was $12.3 million, up from $7.8 million a year earlier.
Worse: day-to-day operations used $15.4 million in cash, versus bringing in $18.7 million in the same quarter of 2025.
Guidance (their own forecast): fourth-quarter sales growth of 15% to 17%, slower than this quarter's 25%.
They sell subscriptions to software that automates work for big companies and governments, plus paid help setting it up.
Sales were $726.9 million in 2025, up from $617.0 million in 2024.
2025 ended with a small profit of $1.2 million, after a loss of $92.3 million in 2024.
Risks they name: one main product, long unpredictable sales, AI rivals, and U.S. federal agencies at 25.3% of sales.
Headlines say third-quarter results beat Wall Street's estimates and the stock jumped 16.6% after the report.
Analysts are split: William Blair upgraded the stock, while a Seeking Alpha writer downgraded it after a big rally.
Appian announced new tools meant to keep AI agents safe and controlled inside business processes.

takeaways: The company is growing fast and now makes a profit, a change from big losses two years ago.
Cash is a weak spot: cash on hand fell from 135,810 to 47,326 (in thousands of dollars) since the end of 2025.
Their own forecast shows growth slowing next quarter, and a big share of sales depends on U.S. government agencies.

points: Argo Blockchain was named in Benzinga lists of tech stocks moving in Monday's pre-market and Tuesday's trading.
These are general market-mover lists. The headlines do not say why the stock moved.
Yahoo Finance UK lists a seasonal returns chart for the stock. That is a past-price tool, not company news.

takeaways: No new earnings report or annual report was in the source, so there is no fresh business news to explain.
The stock showed up in lists of moving stocks, but the headlines give no reason for the move.
A price move on its own does not tell you if the business got better or worse.

earnings.headline: ArcBest's third quarter of 2026 brought higher sales and higher profit than a year ago, though shipment counts slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 15% to $1.2 billion in the third quarter, up from $1.0 billion a year earlier.
Profit (net income) was $51.7 million, or $2.30 per share, up from $39.3 million, or $1.72 per share, a year ago.
Not all good: the trucking network moved 3.0 percent fewer shipments per day, and union wages and fuel pushed costs up.
No number forecast was given. Over nine months, profit was $36,798 thousand, down from $68,214 thousand last year.
ArcBest makes money moving freight: ABF Freight hauls shared-truck loads, MoLo books full trucks, Panther does rush jobs.
It has 14,000 employees and nearly 250 campuses and service centers, and started over a century ago as a local hauler.
Risks it names: hacks or system failures, losing big customers, and a union contract fight or work stoppage.
Other named risks: swings in fuel prices, rising equipment costs, and freight slowdowns when the economy weakens.
Several articles compare ArcBest with other trucking companies, asking whether its shares are fairly priced.
One headline says the chief commercial officer sold $787,707 in company shares.
Coverage notes the quarter beat what analysts expected, while one piece describes a wider freight slump.

takeaways: The latest quarter was clearly better: more sales and more profit, with both parts of the business improving.
The trucking side carried heavier loads but fewer shipments, and its costs rose with wages and fuel.
Profit for the first nine months of the year is still well below last year, so the recovery is recent.

earnings.headline: Alexandria's 3Q26 update focuses on cutting debt and spending, with plenty of cash on hand but a credit outlook marked negative.
points: Sales and profit totals for the quarter weren't in the text we got, so we can't say if they rose or fell.
They say they have $4.6B of cash and credit ready to use (liquidity), and 95.5% of their debt is at a fixed rate.
They expect about $2.6B from selling property and stakes, more than their $1.9B plan, so some sales may slip to 2027.
Bad sign: their debt rating is BBB+ with a Negative outlook, meaning it could be cut. The other rating is Baa2 Stable.
They own and rent out labs and offices to drug, biotech and tech firms, with 340 properties in North America.
Occupancy (share of space rented) was 90.9% at the end of 2025, below their 10-year average of 95%.
A non-cash rent boost from leases bought below market shrank to $41.3 million in 2025 from $89.4 million in 2024.
They had 20 operating buildings up for sale at the end of 2025. One risk they name is inflation.
Many headlines track price targets and daily stock moves. One notes the stock fell 73% over five years.
Another asks whether empty space from leases ending ('dark' lease expirations) will hurt the company's story.

takeaways: The company is selling property and scaling back building plans to lower its debt and spend less.
More of its space is sitting empty than usual, and some leases are ending.
Its debt is long-term and mostly fixed-rate, but one rating agency flagged a possible downgrade.

points: Arqit Quantum shares fell 6.64% in one Tuesday trading session, a headline says. It does not say why.
A MarketBeat page tracks short interest, meaning how many traders are betting the share price will drop.
Arqit shows up in a Motley Fool list of quantum computing stocks, so it is being grouped with that theme.

takeaways: These headlines give no new sales, profit or forecast numbers. They tell you little about how the business is doing.
Most headlines are about share price moves and options charts, not about what the company sells or builds.
Arqit is often talked about as a quantum stock. Price swings like a 6.64% one-day drop show it can move a lot.

earnings.headline: Record orders and a planned merger with Shoals, but a small loss and a lower full-year sales forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $330.2 million this quarter, and the company lost $7.9 million for its common shareholders.
They cut their own 2026 sales forecast (guidance) to $1.34 billion to $1.40 billion, down from $1.4 billion to $1.5 billion.
Record orderbook: $2.6 billion in signed and awarded orders, up 42% from a year ago.
Surprise: they agreed to merge with Shoals Technologies, paying in stock instead of cash.
They make solar 'trackers': motor-driven racks that turn solar panels to follow the sun so the panels make more power.
Sales grew 40% in 2025, but gross margin (profit left after making the product) fell to 23% from 33%.
Higher tariffs (import taxes) raised costs, and sales at their Spain-based STI unit fell 16%. They still lost money for the year.
Biggest risks they name: fitting in bought companies like APA, cuts to solar tax credits, tariffs, and delayed projects.
Most headlines are about the planned stock-for-stock merger with Shoals Technologies.
A law firm, Halper Sadeh, is investigating whether shareholders are getting a fair price in the deal.
Filings show large holders, including one investor with voting power over 14.7M shares.

takeaways: Demand looks strong on paper: orders hit a record, but turning those orders into sales is taking longer than planned.
The company lost money this quarter and lowered its full-year forecast. That is bad news, plainly.
The Shoals merger could change the company a lot, and combining two companies brings its own risks.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 10% to $216.4 million, beating their own forecast, and losses shrank, but the company still lost money.
points: Revenue (sales) was $216.4 million, up 10% from a year ago and above the top of their own forecast (guidance).
Still a loss under standard accounting (GAAP): $39.2 million, smaller than the $48.4 million lost a year earlier.
Next quarter they expect $217 million to $219 million in sales, growth of 8% to 9%, which is slower than this quarter's 10%.
Net retention of 97% means existing customers, as a group, spent a bit less than a year ago. It improved, but it is still a weak spot.
Asana sells work-planning software by subscription to over 180,000 paying customers in 200 countries and territories.
Last fiscal year it still lost $189.0 million, but cash from running the business rose to $90.4 million from $14.9 million.
Much of the loss is stock paid to employees ($214.8 million). It also spent $132.2 million buying back its own shares.
Risks they name: tough competition, adding AI successfully, and moving pricing toward pay-for-what-you-use billing.
Asana shares dropped along with other software stocks like Snowflake and C3.ai; one headline notes a 93% fall over five years.
Writers disagree: some say the stock looks cheap compared with its sales, others say better retention isn't enough yet.
Asana set up a credit line (a loan it can draw on) through 2031, with no money borrowed at the start.

takeaways: The business is improving: sales are growing, losses are shrinking, and it now brings in more cash than it spends.
It is still not profitable under standard accounting, and growth is expected to slow a little next quarter.
Big bets on AI tools and new pricing could help or hurt; existing customers are not yet spending more overall.

earnings.headline: Sales grew to $42.3 million and the company says its satellite plans are on track, but it is still spending far more than it brings in.
points: Revenue (sales) was $42.3 million, from phone-network partners and U.S. government work.
Costs were $211.0 million, far above sales. They fell from $329.1 million mostly because last quarter had a one-time $125.9 million loss.
Adjusted costs (leaving out some non-cash items) rose to $133.6 million from $119.1 million, so day-to-day spending went up.
Guidance (their own forecast) for yearly sales is $150.0 million to $200.0 million. They hold about $3.2 billion in cash.
Their plan: share revenue with phone carriers (over 50 partners, nearly 3 billion subscribers) so normal phones connect from space.
Today, sales come mainly from selling ground equipment to carriers and from work done for the U.S. government.
In February 2026 they borrowed $1,075.0 million with convertible notes, a kind of debt that can later turn into shares.
Risks they name: inflation, supply problems and tariffs could raise the cost to build and launch satellites.
Benzinga reported the stock slid after the quarter missed Wall Street's expectations on two measures.
Other headlines covered drops tied to a tech selloff and Jim Cramer calling it 'a very hard stock to own.'

takeaways: The company is still early: sales are small next to its costs, so it relies on cash on hand and outside funding.
The big test is whether satellites launch on time and spotty service starts by year-end 2026 as planned.
It has about $3.2 billion in cash plus about $1.0 billion in funding from Japan, but it has also taken on more debt.

earnings.headline: AtriCure grew sales 15.0% to $154.5 million and made a profit, after a small loss a year earlier.
points: Sales (money coming in) were $154.5 million, up 15.0% from a year ago. U.S. sales rose 17.1%.
Net income (profit) was $4.1 million, vs. a loss of $0.01 per share a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA (a profit measure) rose 51%.
Guidance (their own forecast): full-year 2026 sales of about $606 million to $610 million.
Bad news: minimally invasive ablation sales fell as doctors switch to PFA catheters, a newer competing heart tool.
They make tools surgeons use for Afib (irregular heartbeat), heart clips, and freezing nerves to ease pain after surgery.
In 2025 sales grew 14.9%, led by pain management (up 32.5%), but the company still lost money for the year.
Minimally invasive ablation sales dropped 31.2% in 2025, a clear weak spot.
Risks they name: competing catheter tools, clinical trial results, tariffs, and getting insurers to pay for procedures.
AtriCure is presenting at the Piper Sandler 38th Annual Healthcare Conference.
A board member sold $143K of company stock, according to a Benzinga report.
One analysis says a new hospital quality measure could lead to more heart clips used in open-heart surgery.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, and the company moved from losing money to making a small profit this quarter.
One older product line is shrinking because doctors are switching to newer catheter tools.
Their forecast is a goal, not a promise. Trial results and competition could change the picture.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit per share rose this quarter, but profit margins in the biggest unit got thinner and one unit's sales fell.
points: Sales were $2.3 billion, up 5.2%. Leaving out currency swings and purchases of other businesses, sales grew 3.7%.
Profit per share was $2.24. Their adjusted figure, which leaves out one-time costs, was $2.42, up 2.1%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 is adjusted profit per share of $10.10 to $10.24.
Weak spots: the Materials unit's profit margin fell to 14.1%, and Solutions unit sales fell 1.8% to $687 million.
They make labels, tapes, graphics films and RFID tags (tiny radio chips that track items), plus software.
There are two parts. Materials Group was about 69% of 2025 sales, and Solutions Group was about 31%.
Profit (net income) fell to about $688 million in 2025, from about $705 million. Lower prices and higher costs hurt.
Biggest risks they name: tariffs and trade fights, wars, currency swings, and raw material costs.
The company offered to buy back some of its bonds (money it borrowed) for cash, and later made that offer bigger.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew a little this quarter, but some profit margins got thinner.
So far this year they gave $481 million back to shareholders through dividends and buying back their own shares.
Cash on hand fell to $271.4 million from $536.3 million. They also name tariffs, wars and costs as risks.

earnings.headline: Official profit held flat at $1.94 a share, while the company's adjusted count rose to $2.00, helped by approved price increases.
points: Sales (revenue) in the water business rose $60 million, mostly from approved price raises. Bad weather cut $18 million.
Costs rose too: operating costs were up $30 million and interest on debt was up $9 million versus a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 is now $6.07 to $6.12 a share, the top half of the old range.
First 2027 forecast: $6.53 to $6.63 a share, about 8% growth. They aim to close the Essential Utilities merger in early 2027.
They sell water and wastewater service to about 14 million people. State regulators (PUCs) set the prices they can charge.
2025 profit was $5.69 a share, up from $5.39. Adjusted, it was $5.64 vs $5.18, mainly from approved rate increases.
Costs climbed: depreciation (wear on pipes and plants) rose $111 million, interest costs rose, and unpaid bills cost $20 million more.
Weather is a swing risk: warmer, drier weather cut sales by an estimated $36 million in 2025. Their debt also keeps growing.
Several articles argue the stock price looks high compared to estimates of what the company is worth.
Analysts both raised and cut their price targets recently. These are opinions, not promises.
The company redesigned its customer website for paying bills, checking service alerts and reporting emergencies.

takeaways: This is a slow, steady business. People always need water, and profits grow mainly when regulators approve higher prices.
Growth costs money. They plan $3.7 billion of spending in 2026, paid partly with more debt, so their interest bills keep rising.
The big change ahead is the merger with Essential Utilities. It still needs more approvals and it adds deal costs along the way.

points: A fund corrected an earlier filing: it now reports owning zero Axonex AI shares, not the 1.4M shares it first disclosed.
A headline says Nixxy announced a 1-for-20 reverse stock split. The headlines don't say how Nixxy is linked to Axonex.
A reverse split swaps many old shares for fewer new ones. It changes the share count and price per share, not the company's total value.

takeaways: There are no earnings or annual report details here, so we can't say how sales or profits are doing.
One fund that was thought to hold 1.4M shares now says it holds none. That is a correction to a filing, not news about the business itself.
A 1-for-20 reverse split under the Nixxy name is in the headlines. These moves often happen when a share price is low, so check the official filings.

points: Two headlines say Barrick's third-quarter (Q3) results were strong. The articles shown here don't give the actual numbers.
One headline says the shares may trade at a premium, meaning a higher price than similar companies, after the Q3 results.
Another headline says the strong Q3 could change the bull case, the optimistic view of the company's future.

takeaways: Recent news says Barrick, a gold and copper miner, had a strong third quarter (Q3), but no actual figures were available here.
These are news headlines, not the company's own report. Check Barrick's official release for real sales and profit figures.
Several headlines in this feed are about other companies with a 'B' in their ticker, not Barrick, so they were left out.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 5% to $2.98 billion and Baxter raised its yearly forecast, but adjusted profit per share fell 16%.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $2.98 billion, up 5%, with growth in every part of the business.
Profit was $298 million ($0.57 a share). Leaving out one-time items: $0.58 a share, down 16%, mostly from a higher tax rate.
They raised their own forecast: yearly sales growth now 4% to 5% (was 3% to 4%), profit per share $2.05 to $2.15.
They paid off $864 million of debt and had $448 million of free cash (cash left after paying for equipment) this quarter.
Baxter sells hospital gear: IV pumps and fluids, surgery products and hospital beds.
2025 sales were $11,244 million, up from $10,636 million, but it lost $957 million after big write-downs and costs.
Its Novum IV pump had serious (Class I) recalls. U.S. shipping was paused, and related costs were about $105 million.
Risks they name: Hurricane Helene cut demand for IV fluids, plus supply problems, tariffs and weak global economic conditions.
Most headlines are stock-price pages and trading chatter, not news about the business itself.
One article looks at how a return to profitability has changed how investors see the company.

takeaways: Sales are growing in every part of the business, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Profit per share fell 16% this quarter, and last year ended with a loss of $957 million.
They are paying down debt, but the IV pump recall, tariffs and supply issues are real risks to watch.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped 2.3% but profit beat the company's own forecast, helped by about $80 million in one-time tariff refunds.
points: Sales were $1,514 million, down 2.3% from $1,549 million. Store sales fell 5.4%; online (Direct) sales rose 3.0%.
Profit (net income) rose to $118 million from $64 million, but about $80 million came from one-time tariff refunds.
Without those refunds, adjusted profit per share would have been $0.31, down from $0.37 a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance): next quarter sales fall 5% to 2.5%, profit per share $0.05 to $0.10 vs $0.37 last year.
They sell body care and home scents like lotion, soap and 3-wick candles in 1,927 U.S. and Canada stores, plus online.
A new CEO, Daniel Heaf, started a multi-year turnaround plan called the Consumer First Formula to win younger shoppers.
Risks they name: weak shopper spending, inflation, tariffs, and leaning heavily on the holiday season for profit.
They warn the turnaround may not work and the spending on it could cut profit in the short term.
Some headlines say shares slid on a weak third-quarter outlook; UBS kept a neutral view.
Its 2026 Advent calendar sold out quickly, per ABC News.
Writers are debating whether the turnaround plan is really working yet.

takeaways: Sales are still shrinking, and the company itself says the business remains under pressure.
Profit looked strong this quarter, but much of the jump came from one-time tariff refunds.
Online sales grew for the first time since 2021, an early sign the turnaround may be helping.

earnings.headline: BD's sales and profit grew this quarter, and it expects slower, steady growth next year after splitting off a big business.
points: Sales (revenue) were $5.3 billion this quarter, up 5.4% from a year ago. For the full year, sales were $19.5 billion.
Profit per share was $2.52 by standard rules, up from $1.20. The adjusted figure, which leaves out one-time costs, was $4.15.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next year: sales growing only a little, and adjusted profit per share of $13.10 to $13.30.
Not every part grew fast. The Connected Care unit's sales grew only 1.6%, much slower than the company overall.
BD makes and sells medical supplies, devices, lab equipment and test products to hospitals, doctors, labs and drug makers.
BD has been fixing or replacing its Alaris infusion pumps (machines that drip medicine into patients) in the U.S. after recalls.
Big risk: its U.S. infusion pump business is under an FDA court order. If it breaks the rules, the FDA can make it stop selling.
Other risks they name: tariffs (import taxes), supply problems, rising costs, stricter European rules and data privacy laws.
BD plans to invest $19 billion in the U.S. over several years, with $3 billion going to building more factories.
Some headlines said the stock dipped before trading opened, even though results beat what analysts expected.
Other headlines point to faster growth in BD's core business as a reason for recent attention.

takeaways: BD sold more and earned more this quarter, but it expects only slow sales growth next year.
The company is now smaller and more focused after handing off its Life Sciences business to Waters.
Regulators still watch its infusion pumps closely, and tariffs and supply costs remain real risks.

earnings.headline: Profit jumped from a year ago as clients added more money for the firm to manage, though part of the jump came from investment gains.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2,434.9 million this quarter, up from $2,343.7 million a year ago.
Profit was $380.1 million, or $0.72 a share, vs $117.6 million a year ago, when a big write-down hit results.
Part of the profit jump came from gains in funds they hold on their own books, which can swing a lot quarter to quarter.
No number forecast (guidance = their own forecast) was given. The CEO expects demand for private investments to keep growing.
They make money by charging fees to manage about $1.8 trillion of other people's money (AUM = assets under management).
Clients added $84.1 billion of new money this year, after pulling out $97.4 billion the year before.
Weak spots: Western Asset lost $11.7 billion to withdrawals, and bond (fixed income) assets shrank this quarter.
Biggest risks they name: market drops, fee pressure, wars, and clients moving to cheaper products like bond funds and ETFs.
Several headlines say the business is turning around as the money it manages rises.
An executive, Matthew Nicholls, sold some of his shares at $36.20 each.
Mizuho, a bank, started covering the stock with a neutral rating.

takeaways: This company earns fees on money it manages, so its results rise and fall with markets and with client deposits.
This year was clearly better: more money came in, and profit roughly doubled to $1,075.3 million from $524.9 million.
Watch the weak spots: bond funds and Western Asset still saw withdrawals, and a market drop would cut their fees.

earnings.headline: Bunge earned more this quarter and kept its full-year forecast, but two of its four business units did worse and cash drained out.
points: Profit per share rose to $1.64 from $0.86 a year ago. Using the company's adjusted math, it was $2.56 vs. $2.27.
Oilseed crushing did well: soybean unit profit rose to $547 million from $337 million; softseed to $353 million from $236 million.
Worse: the tropical oils unit's profit fell to $13 million from $77 million, and the grain unit lost $74 million.
They kept their own full-year forecast (guidance): $9.25 to $9.75 of adjusted profit per share for 2026.
Bunge buys crops like soybeans and canola, crushes them into oil and meal, and moves grain worldwide for food, feed and fuel.
Spending on plants and equipment rose to $1,723 million in 2025 from $1,376 million, partly due to buying Viterra.
Debt is a big load: $3,883 million of short-term debt was due in 2026, plus $1,378 million of long-term debt.
Risks they name: currency swings, changing freight costs that can squeeze profit margins, and cyberattacks.
Most headlines are about daily stock moves versus competitors, not new company events.
Several opinion pieces debate whether the stock looks cheap; those are outside views, not company facts.

takeaways: Profits rose a lot this quarter, mostly from crushing soybeans and other oilseeds in North America.
Not everything improved: tropical oils and grain did worse, and the company expects tropical oils to stay lower.
Cash is a watch item: running the business used $2,302 million in nine months, far more than the $503 million a year ago.

earnings.headline: BILL's sales rose 13% and it swung to a profit, beating its own forecast, but it expects slower sales growth next quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) were $353.8 million, up 13% from a year ago. Subscription and payment fees were $316.4 million, up 14%.
They earned $60.3 million, after losing $3.0 million a year ago. Sales and adjusted profit topped their own forecast.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales growth of 8% - 11%, slower than the 13% they just posted.
New accounting rule: card rewards are now subtracted from sales, so sales look smaller than in old reports. Profit is unchanged.
They make money from monthly fees, a cut of each payment and card swipe, and interest on customer money they hold.
This year they launched AI helpers and BILL Travel, and cut about 30% of staff in May 2026 to save money.
Sales grew to $1.7 billion, but they still lost $11.2 million for the year. Total past losses add up to $2.1 billion.
Risks they name: small-business customers in a weak economy, fraud, unpaid card balances, falling interest rates, and their debt.
Reports say investment firm TPG is close to a deal to buy BILL and take it off the stock market. Not confirmed in the filings.
One headline notes the stock is still down 78% over five years, despite the recent jump.
Other headlines say profits are rising as payment volume keeps growing at double-digit rates.

takeaways: The business is growing, now makes a profit, and beat its own forecast this quarter.
Growth is expected to slow next quarter, and customers slipped to 475,300 from 479,300 in June.
Big job cuts made the company leaner, but it has a long history of losses and real risks.

earnings.headline: More people booked trips (bookings up 10%), but reported sales slipped 1% after a $900 million government charge, and they expect slower growth ahead.
points: Revenue (sales) fell 1% to $8.9B, partly because of a $900 million cut tied to a government (FTC) matter.
Profit (net income) fell 1% to $2.7B. Leaving out one-off items, profit per share rose 17%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for Q4: bookings growth of only 2% - 4%, blaming Middle East disruption and softer travel abroad.
Cash from running the business fell 21% this quarter to $1.1B, though it is up 2% so far this year.
They make money as a middleman, taking a fee when you book hotels, flights or cars on Booking.com, Priceline or Agoda.
Total revenue (sales) for 2025 was $26.9 billion, and they say they hit record room nights that year.
Biggest risk they name: travel drops fast when the economy weakens or wars, unrest or disasters scare people off.
They also warn AI helpers from Google and others could let people book travel without ever visiting their sites.
Several headlines ask whether investors should worry about the company's weaker outlook.
One report says the stock moved down 3.70% on Nov 6, a few days after the results came out.
Other stories focus on its spending on AI travel tools and how it stacks up against rivals.

takeaways: People are still booking more trips with them: room nights grew 7% and total bookings grew 10%.
By their own forecast, next quarter looks slower, mainly because of the Middle East conflict and travel disruptions.
They spent $2.1 billion buying back their own shares this quarter and pay a $0.42 dividend (a cash payment per share).
